title: Ezekiel 27:26–36
context: The lament turns to the wreck. Tyre’s rowers bring the ship into great waters, and the east wind breaks it in the heart of the seas (27:26). Everything named in the earlier verses, riches, wares, mariners, pilots, repairers, soldiers, and company, goes down together (27:27). Sailors abandon their ships, mourn on land with dust, ashes, baldness, and sackcloth, and raise their own lament, “Who is there like Tyre, like her who is brought to silence in the middle of the sea?” (27:28–32). The kings and merchants who had grown rich through Tyre are appalled, the merchants hiss, and the poem ends, “you will be no more” (27:33–36). Revelation 18:9–19 echoes this lament in its picture of kings, merchants, and mariners mourning the fall of Babylon. The wreck is poetic imagery for the city’s conquest, which the LORD announced in 26:7–14; the long campaign of Nebuchadnezzar against Tyre is mentioned again in 29:17–20. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground: the LORD brings down a power that seemed unsinkable, and those who shared its wealth share its grief.

verses.text: Your rowers have brought you into great waters. The east wind has broken you in the heart of the seas.
verses.arminianNotes: “Your rowers have brought you into great waters. The east wind has broken you in the heart of the seas.” Arminian readers note the irony that Tyre’s own rowers steer it into danger, and they hear a warning that the very skill in which a people trusts can carry it toward ruin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the east wind as an instrument of the LORD’s judgment, as it is elsewhere (compare Psalm 48:7), and they read the storm as poetic language for the conquest he announced in 26:7. Shared ground: both traditions read the shipwreck as imagery for the fall of the city, and both affirm that the LORD rules over the winds and the nations.

verses.text: Your riches, your wares, your merchandise, your mariners, your pilots, your repairers of ship seams, the dealers in your merchandise, and all your men of war who are in you, with all your company which is among you, will fall into the heart of the seas in the day of your ruin.
verses.arminianNotes: Everything goes down together: riches, wares, merchandise, mariners, pilots, repairers, dealers, men of war, and all the company “will fall into the heart of the seas in the day of your ruin.” Arminian readers see the inventory of verses 3–25 reversed, as each element of Tyre’s greatness shares in its collapse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sweeping language as a sign that nothing in which Tyre trusted could stand on the day the LORD judged it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sober summary of total loss, and both hear in it the lesson of Psalm 49 and Luke 12:16–21: wealth cannot rescue a person or a people from judgment.

verses.text: At the sound of the cry of your pilots, the pasture lands will shake.
verses.arminianNotes: “At the sound of the cry of your pilots, the pasture lands will shake.” The pilots’ cry carries to the shore, and the coastlands tremble. Arminian readers see the shock of Tyre’s fall spreading far beyond the city, as those who depended on it realize that their own security has been shaken.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the trembling as a picture of how the LORD’s judgment on one power reverberates among the nations (compare the shaking of the islands in 26:15). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as vivid poetic imagery rather than a description of an earthquake, and both see the scene as a public display of the LORD’s judgment.

verses.text: All who handle the oars, the mariners and all the pilots of the sea, will come down from their ships. They will stand on the land,
verses.arminianNotes: “All who handle the oars, the mariners and all the pilots of the sea, will come down from their ships.” They stand on the land. Arminian readers see sailors from many ships abandoning the sea in dismay, as if the world of seafaring had lost its center when Tyre went down.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the mariners as witnesses who confirm the reality of Tyre’s fall; their coming ashore marks the end of an era of trade. Shared ground: both traditions read the scene as the beginning of a public mourning that runs through verse 32, and both see in it the fragility of livelihoods built on a single great power.

verses.text: and will cause their voice to be heard over you, and will cry bitterly. They will cast up dust on their heads. They will wallow in the ashes.
verses.arminianNotes: The mariners “will cry bitterly,” cast dust on their heads, and wallow in the ashes, familiar ancient signs of grief (compare Joshua 7:6; Job 2:12). Arminian readers hear real sorrow in the mourning, and they note that the grief is over lost fortune as much as over the city itself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the rites as the response of those who had invested their hopes in Tyre, and they hear a contrast with mourning that turns to God in repentance (compare Joel 2:12–13). Shared ground: both traditions read the mourning rites as sober, culturally familiar expressions of grief, and both see Revelation 18:19 echoing this scene.

verses.text: They will make themselves bald for you, and clothe themselves with sackcloth. They will weep for you in bitterness of soul, with bitter mourning.
verses.arminianNotes: They “make themselves bald,” put on sackcloth, and weep “in bitterness of soul, with bitter mourning.” Arminian readers see the intensity of grief over a loss the mourners had not imagined possible, and they note that the repeated language of bitterness lingers on the pain of the moment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the mourners’ bitterness the emptiness that follows when security rests on wealth and human greatness rather than on the LORD. Shared ground: both traditions read these rites, which appear in other prophetic laments (compare Isaiah 15:2–3; Jeremiah 48:37), as genuine expressions of sorrow, described without mockery.

verses.text: In their wailing they will take up a lamentation for you, and lament over you, saying, ‘Who is there like Tyre, like her who is brought to silence in the middle of the sea?’
verses.arminianNotes: The mariners raise their own lament: “Who is there like Tyre, like her who is brought to silence in the middle of the sea?” Arminian readers hear a question that once expressed admiration now turned into grief, and they see the city that seemed beyond compare reduced to silence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Scripture often asks who is like the LORD (compare Exodus 15:11; Micah 7:18), and they hear an implied contrast: Tyre was not incomparable, but the LORD is. Shared ground: both traditions read this lament within the lament as the nations’ acknowledgment of Tyre’s fall, and both see Revelation 18:18 echoing it.

verses.text: When your wares came from the seas, you filled many peoples. You enriched the kings of the earth with the multitude of your riches and of your merchandise.
verses.arminianNotes: “When your wares came from the seas, you filled many peoples. You enriched the kings of the earth.” Arminian readers acknowledge that Tyre’s trade brought real benefit to others, and they see the lament recognizing that the loss is felt widely, not by the city alone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see that the kings who grew rich through Tyre were bound to its fortunes, so that its fall exposes a shared trust in wealth among the nations (compare Revelation 18:3). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an honest acknowledgment of Tyre’s former place in the world, and both see the abundance remembered here as the measure of the coming grief.

verses.text: In the time that you were broken by the seas, in the depths of the waters, your merchandise and all your company fell within you.
verses.arminianNotes: “In the time that you were broken by the seas, in the depths of the waters, your merchandise and all your company fell within you.” Arminian readers hear the poem returning to the wreck, and they see the riches that once filled the nations now lying in the depths of the sea.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the contrast between verses 33 and 34 as the heart of the reversal: what once came from the seas is now swallowed by them. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetic imagery for conquest and loss, and both hear it as a warning that no human enterprise lies beyond the reach of the LORD’s judgment.

verses.text: All the inhabitants of the islands are astonished at you, and their kings are horribly afraid. They are troubled in their face.
verses.arminianNotes: “All the inhabitants of the islands are astonished at you, and their kings are horribly afraid. They are troubled in their face.” Arminian readers see the coastal peoples shaken, and they hear in the kings’ fear a recognition that if Tyre could fall, their own security was not assured.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the astonishment as part of the LORD’s purpose in judgment: a public lesson to the nations about the limits of human power (compare 26:16–18). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing the fear that follows the collapse of a great power, and both see it as a call to humility rather than to gloating.

verses.text: The merchants among the peoples hiss at you. You have come to a terrible end, and you will be no more.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: “The merchants among the peoples hiss at you. You have come to a terrible end, and you will be no more.” Hissing was a gesture of shock or derision (compare 1 Kings 9:8; Jeremiah 19:8). Arminian readers hear the end of the lament as a sober warning: a city that boasted of its beauty has become an object of horror.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the closing words the finality of the LORD’s sentence on Tyre’s pride. Readers in both traditions differ on how this language of ending relates to Tyre’s later history; some take it as the idiom of lament, others as fulfilled in stages (compare 26:21). Shared ground: both see the LORD bringing down the proud.
